name: Chloe Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the buying team at Northgate Distribution, which supplies phones, chargers and components to retailers and repair shops. Mornings I read my AI briefing, which summarises supplier news, currency moves and chip shortages, then I check it against my own sources. Then it's negotiations, some by video with factories in Shenzhen and Penang, and a weekly meeting with my five buyers. I finish by reviewing what the model flagged as risky, and decide whether it's right.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the game of it, the moment you find a supplier who's undercutting everyone and you work out why. What wears me out is the pace: product cycles are so short that a wrong guess on 20,000 units can sink a quarter. My partner Rhys, a landscape architect, says I'm the only person he knows who gets excited about the price of capacitors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. I call this one "AI Plateau". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but oversold, which is what I've always said. At work I'd keep showing the team what it's good at, which is summarising and checking, and what it isn't, which is judgement. Online I'd probably roll my eyes at the headlines in both directions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine. My tools save me maybe six hours a week, and that's enough to justify them even if nothing else comes. I'm 58, senior and well paid, so a flat future suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on using my AI tools every day, and keep refining my negotiation prompts. I'd stay on top of the supplier market, and begin planning my exit around 63 with Rhys. We've talked about spending winters somewhere warm, and I'd want to start looking at places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Perhaps even a bit smug, because I've done the work to be ready for either result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI turns out to be mostly hype, you've bet a lot on it. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I haven't bet that much. I use the tools because they work now, not because I believe in a promised land. If they flop, I've lost nothing, since the time saved is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Beyond AI, what's on your mind about work and money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pressures are tariffs, which can wreck a margin overnight, and my mother in a care home that costs a fortune. Also my son Owen, a nurse, works punishing shifts. None of that is about AI, but it's always there.

say: I'd say AI is **useful but oversold**, good at summarising and checking, weak on judgement.
Online I'd roll my eyes at the headlines in both directions.
think: Privately I'm fine: the tools save me about **six hours** a week whatever happens.
A flat future suits me, since I'm senior and well paid.
do: Keep using AI daily and refine my **negotiation prompts**.
Start planning an exit around **63** and look at places for winters somewhere warm.
feel: **Calm**, almost smug, because I'm ready for either result.
S0.quote: I use the tools because they work now, not because I believe in a promised land.
fieldNote: Her **calm** rests on practical use, not belief in hype.
Pressures she named are tariffs, a costly care home for her mother and her son's shifts.
Already thinking about a planned exit at 63.

steps.text: Keep using AI daily and refine my negotiation prompts
Keep checking every supplier risk flag against my own sources
Start looking at winter places for retirement at 63

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. I call this one "Steady Disruption". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the real thing, and the winners will be the people who learn fastest. At work I'd tell the team to treat the tools as a colleague that never sleeps. Online I'd say we need public support and training funds, since not everyone has my head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the task of buying largely moves to software. Reordering, price checks, supplier risk scoring, all of it. My job becomes managing the software and the hard negotiations. I'm not afraid, because I'm already doing that, but I think the team shrinks by half within four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd redesign the team now, before someone does it to us. I'd move two buyers into strategic sourcing and supplier visits, and automate the routine buying with our existing tools. And I'd write a short training course for the rest, which I could also teach outside Northgate for pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with an edge. I'm excited and slightly sad, because I like my buyers and not all of them will want the new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If buying is one of the first things AI takes, where does that leave a head of buying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, who's 31, would do very well, because he's curious. Margaret, who's 55 and a lovely person, is the one I worry about, because she distrusts the tools. I'd sit with her and offer to pair her with Kofi for six months, with no judgement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the five buyers in your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Northgate to keep us all, and fund retraining, in return for the productivity we'll deliver. I'd also keep an eye out for what else I could do, perhaps advising small retailers on using AI. The point is to be one of the people steering this.

say: I'd say this is **real**, and the winners will be those who learn fastest.
Online I'd call for **training funds**, since not everyone has my head start.
think: Privately buying largely moves to software, and the team **halves** within four years.
I'm not afraid, as I'm already doing the **management** work.
do: Redesign the team now, moving two buyers to **strategic sourcing** and visits.
Write a short **training course** that I could also teach outside Northgate for pay.
feel: **Calm** with an edge: excited, and sad that not every buyer will want the new job.
S1.quote: I'd redesign the team now, before someone does it to us.
fieldNote: Adaptive and **ahead** of her team; her confidence is credible.
Cares about Margaret, a colleague who distrusts the tools, and offers a pairing.
Sees a teaching side income in her own expertise.

steps.text: Move two buyers into strategic sourcing and supplier visits
Pair Margaret with Kofi for six months of tool practice
Write an AI buying course to teach outside Northgate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. I call this one "AGI by 2028". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the hardest moment in my working life, and we need a national plan within months. At work I'd be straight with the team. Online I'd say it's no use arguing about whether it's coming, because we'd be too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd expect my own job to go within two years. If a machine can do any thinking work as well or better, then a buyer who negotiates by computer is replaceable. I've got money and skills, but 58 is a hard age to switch, and I'd feel the loss of status.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd talk to Rhys about our spending, then to Northgate about what they plan. I'd bank every spare pound, clear the last of the mortgage, and check our pensions. I'd also start with a charity that helps small firms use AI, so I have a place to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for me alone, but for my children. Tamsin is a graphic designer, and her work will be among the first to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In this picture, what's the thing you'd be most afraid of losing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the sense of being useful. Money I can manage. What I can't replace easily is a team and a reason to get up. I'd also fear for Tamsin, whose freelance income is thin, and I'd help her with rent if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use these tools more than most. Does that help or not help here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps a bit, since I understand what's coming. But it also means I can see how complete it would be. I wouldn't have the comfort of thinking it won't happen to me. It's a strange mix of being prepared and being shaken.

say: I'd say this is the **hardest moment** of my working life and we need a national plan within months.
At work I'd be **straight** with the team.
think: Privately I expect my job to go within **two years**, and 58 is a hard age to switch.
I'd feel the loss of **status** and a team more than the money.
do: Talk to Rhys about **spending**, then clear the last of the mortgage and check our pensions.
Volunteer with a charity helping small firms use **AI**, so I have somewhere to go.
feel: **Anxious**, mostly for my children, since Tamsin's design work would go early.
S2.quote: Money I can manage. What I can't replace easily is a team and a reason to get up.
fieldNote: Her **expertise** gives clarity but no comfort; she sees how complete it would be.
Worry runs to her daughter Tamsin, a freelance designer.
Plans a volunteer role as a landing place.

steps.text: Cut spending and clear the last of the mortgage
Volunteer with a charity helping small firms use AI
Help Tamsin with rent if her freelance work dries up
Press for a national plan by writing to my MP

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. I call this one "AGI by 2031". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift if we use it. At work I'd put together a plan and say it out loud. Online I'd say it should be the biggest policy priority of the decade, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel better because the timing suits me. I'd be 63 and could leave on my terms. For the younger people it would still be hard, but they'd have time to move into things that need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a certificate in AI governance this year, which fits someone who understands procurement. I'd begin consulting on the side for small distributors, one day a week. And I'd save a bit more, so by 63 the choice to stop is mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's the unease of a big deadline, not a threat to my bed at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years lets you see it coming. What would you do with that time that you couldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd just be reacting. With five I can be deliberate, and perhaps do some good. I could help my local college design a course. I'd rather be an adviser than a casualty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change how you think about retiring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably still stop around 63. Rhys and I talked about winters in Portugal, and I'd still want that. But I might do a day or two of advice from there. I wouldn't want to cut off from my field entirely.

say: I'd say five years is **a gift** if we use it, and it should be the top policy priority.
At work I'd put together a plan and **say it out loud**.
think: Privately the timing suits me: I'd be **63** and could leave on my terms.
The younger buyers have time to move into work that **needs a person**.
do: Start a certificate in **AI governance** this year.
Begin **consulting** one day a week for small distributors, and save a little more.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a big deadline, not a threat to my sleep.
S3.quote: With two years I'd just be reacting. With five I can be deliberate, and perhaps do some good.
fieldNote: Time turns her into a **planner** and adviser.
Uses procurement expertise as the basis of a new career.
Still sees herself retiring at 63 with part-time advice.

steps.text: Start a certificate in AI governance this year
Consult one day a week for small distributors
Save extra so stopping at 63 is my choice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. I call this one "AGI by 2036". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's plenty of time to do this properly. At work I'd mentor, and online I'd say let's build the training and safety nets while it's calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm calm. I'd be retired and well off by then, and I like to think I'd have left something behind. My worry is more for my children than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working until 63, take on one or two mentees outside Northgate, and put money into a fund that backs small businesses using AI well. I'd also finish the house and build a studio for Rhys, so we'd be settled before things get strange.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit curious. It's rather exciting if I look at it as someone watching, not as a casualty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A decade is long. What does a good version of it look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good version is one where my children and their friends can still find work that matters, and where we've shared the gains. Tamsin would be doing something good with the new tools, and Owen would be training nurses. And Rhys and I would be somewhere sunny, arguing about a garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger buyers who ask you what to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say study something that makes you hard to replace, such as how people think and what they need. Learn the tools early, because they're the new literacy. And build a network of people who trust you, which no software can fake.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** to build training and safety nets while it's calm.
At work I'd **mentor** anyone who asks.
think: Privately I'm calm: I'd be **retired and well off**, and I worry more for my children.
I find it exciting when I look at it as an observer.
do: Work until **63**, mentor one or two people outside Northgate.
Put money into a fund backing small businesses that use **AI well**, and build Rhys a studio.
feel: **Calm** and curious, even excited, watching rather than suffering.
S4.quote: I'd say study something that makes you hard to replace, such as how people think and what they need.
fieldNote: Ten years makes her a **mentor** rather than a worrier.
Her optimism depends on her money and skills, which she admits.
Advice to the young is practical and tool-friendly.

steps.text: Mentor one or two young buyers outside Northgate
Invest in a fund backing small firms that use AI well
Build Rhys a garden studio before I retire

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most, because nobody would be ready. What would help is a fast national plan and retraining that's paid for by the firms that gain. And for me, a role where I can still help people. I'm not afraid of the change, but of how unevenly it would land.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I know I'm lucky. I'm adaptable, I have savings and I've got Rhys. People who aren't are going to need more than good advice from someone like me.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of the change, but of how unevenly it would land.
portrait: Chloe is a **58-year-old** head of buying at a distributor of phones and components, and uses AI tools every day.
She is progressive and adaptive: she redesigns her team before anyone asks and sees side income in her skills.
She stays calm in gentler worlds, and turns anxious in the two-year world, mostly about status and her daughter's design work.
She blames no one person, but wants fast public plans and retraining funded by firms that gain.
Savings and a steady partner let her plan an exit at 63, with **consulting** and mentoring.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, because nobody would be ready and it would land unevenly.
whatWouldHelp: A fast **national plan** and firm-funded retraining, plus a role where she can still help people.
